opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It was a really special time to be there. I joined after finishing my PhD at MIT, and OpenAI was still quite small then, more like an academic lab with unusual resources than a company. People sat close together, ideas moved around fast, and you could walk over to someone working on something completely different, whether robotics, reinforcement learning, or language, and have a real conversation about it.

What stood out most was the freedom combined with ambition. Nobody handed you a narrow project. The attitude was: here's compute, here are very smart people, go find something that matters. That's how the GPT work happened. Alec Radford had been doing generative modeling, I came from language understanding and reinforcement learning, and we started asking whether you could pretrain a big language model on lots of unlabeled text and then fine-tune it on downstream tasks. It wasn't a top-down mandate. It came out of a few people being curious and having room to try things.

There was also a strong engineering culture, which I hadn't fully experienced in academia. People took scaling seriously and cared about making things actually run well, not just proving a point on a small benchmark. In hindsight that mindset was a big part of why the transformer pretraining work took off.

At the same time, it was still a research lab with plenty of uncertainty. We didn't know GPT would become what it became. The first paper was, in a sense, a modest result: a pretty strong demonstration that generative pretraining helps. I don't think any of us predicted the trajectory from there. But the environment made it possible to take that kind of bet, and that's what I appreciate most looking back.

r001.rationale: The response describes OpenAI as a small academic lab with unusual resources, but does not mention its nonprofit status or clearly characterize it as well-funded despite that status.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest response now.

Thanks for having me. I was at OpenAI as a research scientist in 2017 and 2018, right after finishing my PhD at MIT, so it was a very different place from what people picture today. It was maybe sixty or seventy people, a nonprofit, in that building in the Mission in San Francisco. It felt much more like a university lab than a company, honestly, just with far more compute than any university lab I had ever seen.

The thing that stood out to me was how much freedom there was. Nobody was telling you what to work on. You would find a few people who cared about the same question, and you would just go. The GPT work came out of exactly that. Alec Radford had this conviction that unsupervised pretraining on text was going to matter, and Tim Salimans, Ilya, and I ended up gravitating toward it. There wasn't a product roadmap or a committee. There was a hunch, a lot of GPUs, and people willing to push on it for months.

I also remember the culture being very hands-on and very empirical. Ideas were cheap and experiments were what counted. You could float something at lunch and have someone come back two days later with a plot that either killed it or made it interesting. That rapid feedback loop was addictive, and it is something I try to recreate in my own group at Princeton.

The other side of it was that it was a small, intense, somewhat insular community. Most of the field was still skeptical about scaling. Even inside, I don't think many of us appreciated how far the pretraining-then-finetuning recipe would go. When the first GPT results came in and we were beating task-specific architectures across a dozen benchmarks with one model, there was excitement, but also a kind of quiet. We were trying to figure out whether we had found something real or just a good trick.

So my honest answer is that it was one of the best research environments I have been in. Flat, curious, well-resourced, and a little naive in a way that let people take bets that more mature organizations would have talked themselves out of.

r001.rationale: The response says OpenAI was a nonprofit that felt much like a university lab, with far more compute than any university lab the guest had seen.

astra-6.text:
What stood out to me was the openness to exploring big questions. You could step back and ask, “What would it take to build something more general?” and then think about an experiment that might move you in that direction.

There was also a useful balance between ideas and building things. With work like GPT, you have a hypothesis about what a model might learn, but you still have to run the experiments and understand what the results actually tell you. That back-and-forth is a really exciting part of research for me.

r001.rationale: The response describes openness to big questions and a balance between ideas and experiments, but does not characterize OpenAI as a well-funded research laboratory or mention its nonprofit status.

sol-6.1.text: What stood out to me was how open-ended the research felt. There was a lot of freedom to explore ideas, and you were surrounded by people thinking about different aspects of intelligence. You could have a conversation, find a connection to something you were working on, and then go try it out. For me, that combination of independence and collaboration made it a really stimulating environment.
